We recently brought together researchers from across academia, national labs, healthcare, and policy for the Open Source AI for Science Summit to explore how open models from Meta, such as Muse Glimmer, SAM, DINO v3, TRIBE v2 and UMA, are driving real-world advancements.

A couple highlights:

→ Medical Research: The University of Pittsburgh presented an assistive-robotics system built on DINOv3 and SAM 3. The team plans to demonstrate a robot that can help a person eat and is experimenting with letting users give instructions in their own words.

→ Chemistry: With the University of Chicago, we showed how UMA can simulate entire enzymes, atom by atom, potentially helping scientists understand how they work and engineer better ones for medicine, sustainability and energy.

Vulcan Leo 1 status update:
Follow the latest Vulcan Leo 1 status updates on our mission page:

Based on data received by our Launch Director, we confirm that the Vulcan vehicle launched from Space Launch Complex 41 suffered an anomaly 10 minutes into the flight and failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit. 

Every flight generates data, and every flight teaches us something. Since the anomaly just occurred, we don’t have any specific data yet to understand what occurred today. 

ULA exists to provide assured access to space for our nation and for the customers who depend on us. That purpose is why we take on some of the hardest missions in spaceflight, and why we hold ourselves to the standard of mission success. Today, we did not meet that standard.

We will work closely with our customer and other appropriate organizations to find the cause, determine the appropriate corrective action, and return to flight as quickly as possible.

ULA is committed to full transparency with our customers, and they will have visibility into the investigation process, which utilizes rigorous methodology and corrective action.

We will provide further updates when new information becomes available.

📣 ispace and KDDI Partner to Build a Lunar Communications Network and Enable Future Services 🌕📡

As activities on the Moon and throughout cislunar space continue to expand, the development of infrastructure such as communications and positioning services is becoming increasingly important, in addition to transportation capabilities to and from the lunar surface.

ispace and KDDI have signed a new Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to explore the development of a lunar communications architecture that seamlessly connects the lunar surface, cislunar space, and Earth. The collaboration will combine ispace’s planned Lunar Connect Service with KDDI’s proposed lunar communications ground stations, lunar mobile communications, and optical space communications technologies.

As a first step, ispace is planning to launch its first lunar-orbiting satellite into lunar orbit as Mission 2.5, with the earliest launch targeted for 2027.

Furthermore, the two companies will work together on initiatives that contribute to Cislunar Security through the realization of a lunar communications network that Japan can independently operate, as well as on space industry promotion and talent development in Yamaguchi Prefecture.
